waves.statement: A periodic wave moving at speed v has wavelength λ and frequency f connected by v = fλ. Changing the medium may change wave speed and wavelength while the source frequency stays fixed. Use metres and seconds to obtain speed in m/s.
waves.workedExample: A 2 Hz wave with wavelength 3 m moves at 2 × 3 = 6 m/s using wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
waves.exercise: What is the speed of a 5 Hz wave with wavelength 4 m?

waves.subject: physics
waves.title: Sound needs matter
waves.statement: Sound is a mechanical wave caused by vibrating matter. It travels through gases, liquids and solids but cannot propagate through vacuum. Light is electromagnetic radiation and can travel through vacuum, illustrating that not every wave has the same physical requirements.
waves.workedExample: A ringing object can be heard through air but sound cannot travel between planets through empty space.
waves.exercise: Why is a silent vacuum different from transparent vacuum?
waves.answer: Sound needs a material medium; light does not.

waves.subject: physics
waves.title: Reflections and echoes
waves.statement: Waves may reflect at a boundary, change direction or be absorbed. A sound echo is a reflected wave arriving after a delay sufficiently long to be perceived separately. The travel time depends on the speed and the outward-and-return path length.
waves.workedExample: An echo from a distant wall is heard after the original shout because sound travels to the wall and back.
waves.exercise: Why is the wall distance not equal to the full echo travel distance?
waves.answer: Sound travels both to the wall and back, covering twice the distance.

waves.subject: physics
waves.title: Transverse and longitudinal vibrations
waves.statement: For a transverse wave the disturbance oscillates perpendicular to the direction of propagation; for a longitudinal wave it oscillates parallel to that direction. These are models of disturbance directions, not a claim that the medium moves permanently with the wave.
waves.workedExample: A pulse along a stretched rope may be transverse, while sound in air is approximately longitudinal.
waves.exercise: Which wave type has vibrations parallel to its travel direction?

waves.subject: physics
waves.title: Waves at a boundary
waves.statement: When a wave reaches a boundary, part of its energy may be reflected, transmitted or absorbed. The proportions depend on the materials and the wave properties. Observing a reflected pulse helps identify the boundary and the time needed to travel there and back.
waves.workedExample: A wave pulse on a rope may return after reaching an anchored end.
waves.exercise: Why might the amplitude of a reflected pulse be lower than the incident pulse?
waves.answer: Some energy can be transmitted, absorbed or dissipated at the boundary.

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Electric charge and attraction
electric.statement: Matter contains positive and negative electric charges. Opposite charges attract and like charges repel; neutral objects may also be attracted when their charges redistribute through polarisation. Frictional charging transfers charge rather than creating it from nothing.
electric.workedExample: A rubbed balloon can attract small neutral paper pieces through charge redistribution.
electric.exercise: Are newly charged objects created by making new electrons?
electric.answer: No; existing charges are transferred or redistributed.

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Current is charge flow
electric.statement: Electric current is the amount of electric charge passing a point per unit time, measured in amperes. A current needs a conducting pathway and an appropriate energy source to remain sustained. Current and electron speed are not the same physical quantity.
electric.workedExample: An electric current of 1 A corresponds to 1 coulomb of charge passing per second.
electric.exercise: What physical quantity is measured in amperes?
electric.answer: Electric current, or charge flow rate.

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Potential difference
electric.statement: Electric potential difference describes the energy transfer per unit charge between two points. It is measured in volts. A voltage does not guarantee a particular current without knowing the circuit and the materials involved.
electric.workedExample: A 6 V battery can support different currents through different resistive circuits.
electric.exercise: Why cannot voltage alone tell you the current?
electric.answer: Current depends also on resistance and circuit conditions.

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Resistance of a conductor
electric.statement: Electrical resistance measures opposition to current in a chosen circuit model. In an ohmic component, current equals voltage divided by resistance at suitable constant conditions. Many devices are not perfectly ohmic over their whole operating range.
electric.workedExample: With 12 V across a 4 Ω resistor, the ideal current is I = V/R = 12/4 = 3 A, assuming approximately constant resistance.
electric.exercise: What ideal current flows at 9 V across 3 Ω?

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Conductors and insulators
electric.statement: A conductor permits electric charge to move readily under an electric field, while an insulator opposes such movement under ordinary conditions. Properties vary with material and environment. An insulating coating does not make a dangerous electrical source suitable for a classroom experiment.
electric.workedExample: Copper conducts electricity; many plastics are useful cable insulators.
electric.exercise: Why is a metal wire often coated in plastic?
electric.answer: The coating helps prevent unintended contact with the conducting core.

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Electric safety
electric.statement: Electricity investigations should use supervised low-voltage educational equipment or simulations. Household mains circuits can cause injury even when an experiment looks simple. Never place conductive objects into sockets or attempt to test an unknown circuit by touch.
electric.workedExample: A classroom simulation can illustrate current and resistance without connection to a wall socket.
electric.exercise: Why is a home power socket unsuitable for pupils’ resistance experiments?
electric.answer: Mains electricity can cause severe injury; use safe low-voltage equipment or simulations.

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Charge, voltage and energy
electric.statement: Voltage is energy transferred per unit electric charge between two points. Current measures charge passing each second; the two quantities answer different questions. A source of higher voltage does not necessarily deliver more current to every possible load.
electric.workedExample: A 9 V battery transfers 9 joules per coulomb of charge moving through the appropriate potential difference.
electric.exercise: What is the SI unit of potential difference?
electric.answer: The volt, equivalent to one joule per coulomb.

electric.subject: physics
electric.title: Resistivity and wire dimensions
electric.statement: Resistance of an ordinary conducting wire depends on material, length, cross-sectional area and temperature. A longer wire of the same material and thickness commonly has greater resistance. The approximation for a uniform wire requires comparable conditions.
electric.workedExample: Two copper wires of identical thickness but different lengths may have different resistances.
electric.exercise: If copper wire length doubles at unchanged temperature and area, how does resistance change?
electric.answer: It approximately doubles for a uniform wire.

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Open and closed paths
circuits.statement: A simple circuit requires a complete conducting path for steady current to flow. Opening a switch breaks the path and typically stops the current in that branch. The circuit diagram shows connections, not the exact physical size or shape of each component.
circuits.workedExample: A bulb connected to a battery can light with a closed switch and turn off when the switch opens.
circuits.exercise: What changes when the only switch in a simple circuit opens?
circuits.answer: The conducting path is broken, stopping current through the bulb.

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Circuit symbols
circuits.statement: Circuit diagrams use agreed symbols for sources, switches, lamps and resistors. They help compare electrical connections and identify series or parallel arrangements. The order of symbols on the page does not always indicate the physical location of the actual components.
circuits.workedExample: Two diagrams drawn differently may still describe identical connections of battery, switch and lamp.
circuits.exercise: Why use symbols instead of photographs to represent a circuit?
circuits.answer: Standard symbols show electrical connections clearly and consistently.

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Resistors in series
circuits.statement: In a series circuit the same current passes through each component along one path. Ideal resistances add: total resistance equals the sum of individual resistances. Removing one component may open the only path.
circuits.workedExample: Two 3 Ω resistors in series have an equivalent resistance of 6 Ω.
circuits.exercise: What is the equivalent resistance of 4 Ω and 5 Ω in series?

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Resistors in parallel
circuits.statement: Parallel branches share the same potential difference across their endpoints. Total current is the sum of branch currents, and the equivalent resistance of positive ideal resistors is less than either branch resistance. Each branch can have different current.
circuits.workedExample: Two equal 4 Ω resistors in parallel give a total resistance of 2 Ω.
circuits.exercise: Can two parallel branches have different currents despite equal voltage?
circuits.answer: Yes; the currents depend on their branch resistances.

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Measuring current and voltage
circuits.statement: An ammeter normally measures current in series with a component, while a voltmeter measures potential difference in parallel across it. Connecting instruments incorrectly can alter a circuit or damage equipment. School exercises should use safe low-voltage apparatus.
circuits.workedExample: A voltmeter is connected across the two terminals of a resistor to measure its voltage.
circuits.exercise: How is a voltmeter connected across a bulb?
circuits.answer: In parallel, between the two bulb terminals.

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Electric power in circuits
circuits.statement: Electrical power is energy transfer per unit time. In suitable DC circuits, power equals potential difference multiplied by current, with watts as the unit. Energy consumed depends on power and the period of operation.
circuits.workedExample: A component with 6 V across it and current 0.5 A uses power 3 W.
circuits.exercise: What power corresponds to 12 V and 2 A?

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Current at a junction
circuits.statement: Charge conservation means current entering a junction in a steady circuit equals the sum of currents leaving it. This rule allows simple branch-current calculations without assuming identical currents in parallel components of unequal resistance.
circuits.workedExample: If 3 A enters a junction and 1 A leaves one branch, 2 A must leave through the other branch.
circuits.exercise: If 5 A enters and two outgoing branches have 2 A and an unknown current, what is the unknown?
circuits.answer: 3 A, so outgoing currents total 5 A.

circuits.subject: physics
circuits.title: Ohm’s law in practice
circuits.statement: For a resistor behaving approximately ohmically at fixed conditions, V=IR. A worked answer should show rearrangement, substitution with units and a check for plausibility. Diodes, lamps and other components may not follow a constant-resistance model over their full range.
circuits.workedExample: For 12 V and 6 Ω, an ideal ohmic resistor carries I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A. The calculation assumes constant resistance.
circuits.exercise: An ideal 5 Ω resistor has 15 V across it; what current flows?

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Magnetic poles
electromagnetism.statement: A magnet has north and south poles, and two like poles repel while unlike poles attract. The terms describe the pattern of interaction rather than separate, isolated magnetic charges. Iron and several other materials can be strongly affected by magnets.
electromagnetism.workedExample: The north pole of one bar magnet repels the north pole of another.
electromagnetism.exercise: What happens when two south poles approach each other?

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Field around a magnet
electromagnetism.statement: A magnetic field describes the influence of a magnet in space and has a direction. A compass needle tends to align with the local magnetic field. Nearby metal objects or other magnets can interfere with the observation.
electromagnetism.workedExample: A compass placed around a bar magnet points in different directions as its position changes.
electromagnetism.exercise: Does a compass directly measure the strength of a magnet in newtons?
electromagnetism.answer: No; it responds mainly to the local magnetic field direction.

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Magnetic effect of current
electromagnetism.statement: An electric current produces a magnetic field around a conductor. The pattern depends on conductor geometry and current direction. Reversing current reverses the field direction for the same arrangement. Investigations must use safe low-voltage equipment.
electromagnetism.workedExample: A compass near a wire can deflect when the wire carries a current.
electromagnetism.exercise: What happens to the field direction when current direction reverses?
electromagnetism.answer: The magnetic field direction reverses for the same geometry.

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Solenoids and coils
electromagnetism.statement: A current-carrying coil produces a magnetic field whose pattern resembles a bar magnet when suitably arranged. More turns or a suitable magnetic core may increase its strength, but heating and material limitations also matter. A coil is not a permanent magnet merely because it has turns.
electromagnetism.workedExample: A coil around a soft-iron core can attract small paper clips while a safe current flows.
electromagnetism.exercise: Why does a solenoid lose much of its magnetic effect when switched off?
electromagnetism.answer: The magnetic field due to current ceases and a soft core loses most induced magnetisation.

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Electromagnets in devices
electromagnetism.statement: Electromagnets are useful where a magnetic field must be controlled by electricity. Relays, lifting magnets and some motors use interactions between currents and magnetic fields. Device construction depends on suitable engineering and safety measures.
electromagnetism.workedExample: A relay can use a current-carrying coil to move a contact without direct mechanical input from the control switch.
electromagnetism.exercise: What advantage does an electromagnet have over a fixed permanent magnet?
electromagnetism.answer: Its magnetic effect can be controlled by changing the supplied current.

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Changing fields and induction
electromagnetism.statement: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit can induce an electromotive force. The direction follows a rule opposing the change that creates it, consistent with conservation of energy. The effect is a foundation for generators and transformers, not a source of energy from nothing.
electromagnetism.workedExample: Moving a magnet through a coil can produce a voltage across the coil terminals.
electromagnetism.exercise: Why does an electrical generator still require mechanical energy input?
electromagnetism.answer: Electrical output comes from work done to change the magnetic flux, not from creating energy.

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Electromagnetic motors
electromagnetism.statement: Electric motors use forces on currents in magnetic fields to create rotation. The interaction depends on current, field direction and geometry. A motor transfers electrical energy into mechanical movement, with some energy also transferred as heat and sound.
electromagnetism.workedExample: An electric fan uses a motor to rotate its blades. Electrical input drives mechanical rotation while some energy becomes heat and sound.
electromagnetism.exercise: Does a motor create mechanical energy without an energy input?
electromagnetism.answer: No; it converts and transfers energy supplied to it.

electromagnetism.subject: physics
electromagnetism.title: Transformers and changing fields
electromagnetism.statement: A transformer uses changing magnetic flux to transfer energy between circuits. In the ordinary model it requires a varying current rather than a constant DC current. The number of turns helps determine voltage relationships under suitable ideal assumptions.
electromagnetism.workedExample: A mains transformer can change AC voltage while transferring energy electromagnetically between coils.
electromagnetism.exercise: Can an ideal ordinary transformer change steady DC voltage just by connecting two coils?
electromagnetism.answer: No; a changing magnetic field is required for induced voltage.

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Choosing the right instrument
measurement.statement: A measurement compares a physical quantity with a unit using an appropriate instrument. A ruler measures length, a stopwatch measures duration and a thermometer measures temperature. A measurement made with the wrong instrument cannot be rescued by extra decimal places.
measurement.workedExample: Use a stopwatch rather than a kitchen scale to time a moving toy.
measurement.exercise: Which instrument would you choose to measure a short time interval?

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Reading an instrument scale
measurement.statement: The smallest marked division and correct alignment affect what can be read from a scale. View the scale correctly to avoid parallax error. Recording a value to an unjustified number of decimal places gives an impression of precision not supported by the tool.
measurement.workedExample: A ruler marked in centimetres alone cannot justify a measurement to hundredths of a millimetre.
measurement.exercise: What should be checked before reading a graduated scale?
measurement.answer: Its division size, units, zero point and viewing angle.

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Repeating observations
measurement.statement: Repeated measurements show how a result varies under similar conditions. The mean summarises the observations but cannot remove every systematic error. Preserve the actual readings so another person can check the work.
measurement.workedExample: Three durations of 4 s, 5 s and 6 s give a mean of (4+5+6)/3 = 5 s. Keep all readings to show the spread around the mean.
measurement.exercise: What is the mean of 5 s, 7 s and 9 s?

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Uncertainty and bias
measurement.statement: Random variation causes readings to differ, whereas a systematic error shifts them consistently. Repeating a biased measurement does not eliminate the bias. Compare an instrument with a suitable known reference when calibration is uncertain.
measurement.workedExample: A timer that always starts one second late may produce consistently wrong durations.
measurement.exercise: Can repeating a miscalibrated instrument remove all bias?
measurement.answer: No; systematic errors require correction or recalibration.

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Tables and graphs
measurement.statement: A data table should name quantities and include units. A scientific graph needs labelled axes and an appropriate scale. Reading the graph requires checking what each axis represents and whether data points support the suggested trend.
measurement.workedExample: Plot distance in metres against time in seconds to compare two toy-car movements.
measurement.exercise: What must be written on each graph axis?
measurement.answer: The physical quantity, its unit and a readable scale.

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Testing a prediction
measurement.statement: A scientific prediction can be checked through observations or experiments. A fair comparison should hold other influential conditions as constant as practical. A disagreement between result and prediction is useful information, not permission to rewrite the data.
measurement.workedExample: To test a ramp slope, use the same trolley and surface while changing ramp inclination.
measurement.exercise: Why should the trolley and surface remain the same in a slope test?
measurement.answer: To help isolate the effect of the changed ramp angle.

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Controlled and measured variables
measurement.statement: A fair investigation distinguishes an independent variable deliberately changed, a dependent variable measured and other conditions held stable. Without this distinction, a reported trend may be explained by several uncontrolled factors.
measurement.workedExample: To study the effect of ramp height on journey time, keep the trolley and surface the same while changing ramp height.
measurement.exercise: Which variable is dependent in the ramp-height experiment?

measurement.subject: physics
measurement.title: Reliability and validity
measurement.statement: Reliable results can be repeated consistently; valid investigations actually test the stated question. A precise instrument cannot make a badly designed comparison valid if an important factor changes between trials. Both design and measurements need scrutiny.
measurement.workedExample: Changing both the trolley mass and ramp height would confuse an investigation of only ramp height.
measurement.exercise: What is one way to improve validity when testing the effect of ramp angle?
measurement.answer: Hold other influential conditions, including trolley and track surface, as constant as practical.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Internal energy
thermodynamics.statement: Internal energy describes microscopic kinetic and potential contributions within a system. It differs from temperature, which characterises thermal state. Work and heating can change internal energy without needing a chemical reaction.
thermodynamics.workedExample: Rubbing two surfaces can warm them through frictional energy transfer.
thermodynamics.exercise: Is the internal energy of an object equal to its temperature?
thermodynamics.answer: No; temperature and internal energy are different quantities.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Specific heat capacity
thermodynamics.statement: Specific heat capacity describes the energy needed per unit mass for a unit temperature rise under specified conditions. A simplified relation is Q=m c ΔT without phase change; using mass in kilograms and c in J/(kg·K) gives energy in joules.
thermodynamics.workedExample: For the same mass and temperature rise, a larger specific heat capacity requires more heating energy.
thermodynamics.exercise: What does c represent in Q=m c ΔT?
thermodynamics.answer: Specific heat capacity of the material.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Thermal equilibrium
thermodynamics.statement: Energy flows spontaneously by heating between bodies at different temperatures until an equilibrium state is approached, provided no additional source maintains the difference. The final temperature depends on masses, materials and transfers to the surroundings.
thermodynamics.workedExample: Warm water mixed with cooler water usually reaches an intermediate temperature if losses are small.
thermodynamics.exercise: Is the final mixture temperature always the arithmetic mean of the two initial temperatures?
thermodynamics.answer: No; masses and heat capacities matter.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Change of phase
thermodynamics.statement: Melting, freezing, boiling and condensation involve changing physical states. At fixed pressure, energy can be absorbed or released while temperature remains approximately constant during a pure substance’s phase transition. The chemical identity need not change.
thermodynamics.workedExample: Ice at its melting point absorbs energy while becoming liquid water.
thermodynamics.exercise: Why can heating ice at its melting point fail to raise its temperature immediately?
thermodynamics.answer: The transferred energy is used for the phase change.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Conservation in thermal transfers
thermodynamics.statement: In an isolated system, total energy is conserved. Thermal calculations can balance energy lost by one object with energy gained by another, but real containers often exchange energy with air or the apparatus. Assumptions must be stated before computing a final temperature.
thermodynamics.workedExample: If hot and cold samples exchange energy in an ideal insulated container, their transfers balance.
thermodynamics.exercise: Why may a measured mixing temperature differ from a simple theoretical prediction?
thermodynamics.answer: Heat loss to the surroundings, the container and measurement uncertainty can matter.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Efficiency of heating devices
thermodynamics.statement: A heating device transfers energy from a source into its surroundings or target. Efficiency compares useful heating with the total input, and depends on the defined system boundary. No device creates energy merely by producing a high temperature.
thermodynamics.workedExample: An insulated kettle can reduce energy wasted heating the surrounding air.
thermodynamics.exercise: How could adding insulation improve the useful fraction of energy transfer?
thermodynamics.answer: It can reduce energy escaping to the surroundings.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Particle model of gases
thermodynamics.statement: Gas pressure arises from particles colliding with container walls. Heating a gas can increase particle kinetic energy, but the resulting changes in pressure or volume depend on whether the container can expand and on other conditions.
thermodynamics.workedExample: A rigid sealed container may show rising gas pressure as temperature increases, within a suitable model.
thermodynamics.exercise: Does gas pressure always stay unchanged when a sealed rigid container is heated?
thermodynamics.answer: No; its pressure generally increases as temperature rises.

thermodynamics.subject: physics
thermodynamics.title: Thermal efficiency and insulation
thermodynamics.statement: Insulation can reduce transfer of thermal energy to the surroundings. The benefit depends on conduction, convection, radiation, surface area and exposure time; an insulated container is not a source of new energy. An energy comparison should state which transfers are useful.
thermodynamics.workedExample: A vacuum flask reduces several heat-transfer pathways, helping a drink stay warm longer.
thermodynamics.exercise: Does a thermos keep a drink warm by continuously creating heat?
thermodynamics.answer: No; it slows unwanted energy transfers to the surroundings.
